intro: Imagine cutting a path for water straight through a mountain, by hand. You are at the Vespasian–Titus Tunnel, a monument in Hatay province from the 1st century AD. This 1.4-kilometre Roman diversion tunnel was cut through solid rock to keep floodwater out of the harbour of Seleucia Pieria.
history: To understand this tunnel, start with the harbour. Seleucia Pieria was the port of Antioch, and floodwater pouring off the mountain behind it kept silting that harbour up. The answer, begun under Vespasian, was bold: cut clean through the mountain and throw the water into the sea beside the port. There were no explosives. The tunnel was carved with hammer and chisel, and inscriptions record who did the work: Roman soldiers and convicts.
highlights: As you wander, don't miss the tunnel mouth, then follow the channel and watercourse. Look out for the Beşikli Cave tombs, and be sure to find the Vespasian–Titus inscription.
facts: Did you know? The tunnel took roughly a century to finish, and the inscription at its mouth names both Vespasian, who began it, and Titus, who completed it. It runs 1,380 metres and stands up to seven metres high in places, all of it cut by hand with hammer and chisel — the largest known diversion tunnel of the ancient world. Digging began from both ends at once, and the teams met inside the mountain; look closely and you can still see, with the naked eye, the slight misalignment where they joined. Finally, the Beşikli Cave at the tunnel's outflow is a Roman necropolis of twelve rock-cut burial chambers.
outro: Our journey through the Vespasian–Titus Tunnel ends here. Before you go, a small request: please leave the stones untouched, keep to the marked paths and carry water with you. Every chisel mark here was made by hand; let them stay for those who come after you. Enjoy your visit.
